newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU SEEKS TO EMBRACE ALL IN ENLARGEMENT PLAN.
newsitem.headline: EU SEEKS TO EMBRACE ALL IN ENLARGEMENT PLAN.

text.p: The European Union, keeping a firm distance from NATO's expansion plans, stressed on Sunday that countries left out of its first enlargement wave would not be excluded from the European family.

A two-day meeting of EU foreign ministers agreed in principle to a plan for a standing conference of EU candidates, stressing it wanted to make all hopefuls, whatever their readiness for EU membership, feel embraced by the EU project.

European Commission President Jacques Santer acknowledged at a news conference that some of the 10 eastern European countries queueing at the EU's door might not be deemed ready to start immediate entry talks when the Commission reports in July.
"Some...will find it easier to accede than others," he said, after ministers met in the Dutch country town of Apeldoorn.
He said the conference plan could help prevent a feeling of exclusion. "We would have them all together so there can be no rift between those in the first wave and those in the second."

"The idea is to set it up in such a way that it's inclusive," Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, who hosted the meeting, told the news conference of the plan, a loose concept which will now be fleshed out.

The idea arose during talks about one of the EU's biggest long-term foreign policy dilemmas -- whether to open negotiations with all, or just the adequately prepared, of the 10 eastern countries pinning their hopes on eventual membership of the rich western club.

Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria, Romania, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have all been promised eventual EU membership, but only a handful are seen as up to scratch at present.

The ministers were unswayed by worries at NATO -- itself preparing at its July summit to offer talks to an avant-garde of one-time foes from behind the former Iron Curtain -- that a double rejection could alienate some countries struggling to distance themselves from their Soviet past.
Unwilling to act as a compensation prize for NATO rejects, the ministers shunned a formal link between the two projects.
"We feel that the enlargement of the European Union and the expansion of NATO constitute two separate but complementary processes," Santer told the news conference.
It remains to be seen who exactly will be invited to the forum, which could discuss issues like environmental policy and the fight against organised crime.

Some suggested it should also embrace countries whose EU applications are not being actively pursued -- as is the case with Norway and Switzerland - or those whicho may apply in the future, like Croatia and Albania.
Ministers remained non-committal about whether to invite Turkey, a NATO ally bitterly resentful of being left out of the EU plans, while former enemies are being taken on board.
While the ministers asked the European Commission to examine ways of strengthening links with Ankara they stopped short of making a promise it would be invited to the conference.
The EU concedes that Ankara has a European future but its credentials are harmed by its economy and human rights record. 161602 GMT mar 97
